youtube.title: Narva, Estonia: The NATO Border City Where Only 4% Are Estonian
youtube.description:
Narva, Estonia is a NATO and EU town on the Russian border, where a medieval castle faces the Russian fortress of Ivangorod across about 150 metres of river. Only about 4 in 100 people here are ethnic Estonians, and most speak Russian. How did a NATO town end up speaking Russian, and why do analysts say the alliance watches it so closely?

This video maps the river today, shows how the line here was fortified, erased, moved and restored from 1492 to 1991, sets out Estonia's case and Russia's case in their own terms, and walks through three ways the map here could change.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: If you lived in Narva, which bank of the river would feel like home, and why? 👇

sources.claim: Two castles face each other across about 150 metres of the Narva River
sources.source: Narva Museum (Hermann Castle) visitor information; distance measured on Estonian Land Board map, 2026

sources.claim: Narva is in Estonia, a member of NATO since 29 March 2004 and of the EU since 1 May 2004
sources.source: NATO, member countries page; European Union, EU enlargement 2004

sources.claim: Only about 4 in 100 people in Narva are ethnic Estonians
sources.source: Statistics Estonia, Population and Housing Census 2021, ethnic nationality by municipality

sources.claim: NATO has 32 members; an attack on one is treated as an attack on all
sources.source: North Atlantic Treaty, Article 5 (1949); NATO member list since Sweden joined, 7 March 2024

sources.claim: Estonia has about 1.4 million people
sources.source: Statistics Estonia, population on 1 January 2025

sources.claim: Estonia's border with Russia runs about 324 kilometres
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, Estonia, land boundaries

sources.claim: The Narva River flows 77 kilometres from Lake Peipus to the Gulf of Finland
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Narva River'

sources.claim: St Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, is about 135 km from Narva in a straight line; Tallinn about 190 km
sources.source: Great-circle distances measured between city centres, 2026; Rosstat population figures

sources.claim: About 54,000 people live in Narva, Estonia's third-largest city
sources.source: Statistics Estonia, Population and Housing Census 2021

sources.claim: In Ida-Viru County Russian speakers are the majority; in Narva most people's first language is Russian
sources.source: Statistics Estonia, Census 2021, mother tongue by county and municipality

sources.claim: About 69 percent of Estonia's people are ethnic Estonians
sources.source: Statistics Estonia, Census 2021 (69.1%)

sources.claim: Roughly half of Narva holds Estonian citizenship and about a third Russian citizenship
sources.source: Statistics Estonia, Census 2021, citizenship by municipality; figures vary by year

sources.claim: Hermann Castle was begun under Danish rule in the 1200s
sources.source: Narva Museum, history of Hermann Castle

sources.claim: Ivangorod Fortress was built for Ivan III of Moscow in 1492
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ivangorod'

sources.claim: Before 1492 the Narva River was already the boundary between Livonia and the Russian lands of Novgorod
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Narva' and 'Ivangorod'; Kasekamp, A History of the Baltic States (2010)

sources.claim: The Friendship Bridge is about 160 metres long
sources.source: Estonian Transport Administration, Narva Friendship Bridge (162 m)

sources.claim: Since 1 February 2024 Russia's Ivangorod crossing has been closed to vehicles for reconstruction
sources.source: ERR News, 'Russia to close Ivangorod border crossing to vehicles', January 2024

sources.claim: Oil-shale power stations near Narva for decades made most of Estonia's electricity
sources.source: Eesti Energia annual reports; IEA, Estonia 2023 Energy Policy Review

sources.claim: In 1934 Narva was about two thirds Estonian
sources.source: Estonian state census 1934 (Rahvaloendus 1934), Narva town results

sources.claim: In the 1400s Narva was a town of the Livonian Order
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Narva'

sources.claim: Russia took Narva in 1558; Sweden took it in 1581 and held it until 1704, when Peter the Great took it
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Narva'

sources.claim: Charles XII beat a far larger Russian army at Narva in November 1700, attacking in a snowstorm
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Battle of Narva'

sources.claim: The region passed to Russia under the Treaty of Nystad, 1721; both banks then lay inside the Russian Empire until 1918, with no international border on the river
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Treaty of Nystad' and 'Narva'

sources.claim: Estonia declared independence on 24 February 1918 and fought until 1920
sources.source: Andres Kasekamp, A History of the Baltic States (2010)

sources.claim: Treaty of Tartu, 2 February 1920: Russia recognised Estonia's independence and renounced sovereign rights for ever
sources.source: Peace Treaty of Tartu, Article II, 2 February 1920

sources.claim: The 1920 border ran east of the river, so Ivangorod was in Estonia
sources.source: Kasekamp, A History of the Baltic States (2010); Estonian Land Board historical maps

sources.claim: The Soviet Union occupied Estonia in 1940 under the secret protocol of the 1939 pact with Nazi Germany
sources.source: Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact secret protocol, 23 August 1939; Kasekamp (2010)

sources.claim: In 1944 the front ran through Narva for months and the old town was almost destroyed
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Narva'; Narva Museum

sources.claim: In November 1944 Moscow moved Ivangorod and the land east of the river to the Russian SFSR
sources.source: Decree of the Presidium of the USSR Supreme Soviet, November 1944; Kasekamp (2010)

sources.claim: Estonia also lost the Petseri area, about 5 percent of its pre-war land
sources.source: Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Estonia-Russia border background

sources.claim: After the war most pre-war residents were not allowed to return
sources.source: Narva Museum; Kasekamp, A History of the Baltic States (2010)

sources.claim: Workers came from across the USSR for rebuilt factories and the Kreenholm textile mill
sources.source: Narva Museum; Kasekamp (2010)

sources.claim: Estonia restored independence on 20 August 1991
sources.source: Riigikogu, resolution of 20 August 1991

sources.claim: The line here was fortified in 1492, lost as an international border from 1721, set east of the river in 1920, moved back to the river in 1944 and made international in 1991
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ivangorod', 'Treaty of Nystad'; Kasekamp (2010); Riigikogu, 20 August 1991

sources.claim: Estonia gave automatic citizenship to pre-1940 citizens and their descendants
sources.source: Estonian Citizenship Act (1938 law restored, February 1992)

sources.claim: Many Soviet-era arrivals had to pass a language exam; many were left stateless with grey alien's passports
sources.source: Estonian Police and Border Guard Board; Kasekamp (2010)

sources.claim: Narva's July 1993 autonomy referendum: about 97 percent yes, turnout about 54 percent; Estonia's Supreme Court ruled it unlawful
sources.source: Kasekamp (2010); New York Times reporting, July 1993

sources.claim: A border treaty was signed in 2005; Russia withdrew its signature after Estonia's parliament added a reference to the 1920 treaty
sources.source: Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs; BBC News, September 2005

sources.claim: The treaty was signed again on 18 February 2014 and has not been ratified
sources.source: Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs; ERR News

sources.claim: Putin, 18 March 2014: 'the Russian nation became one of the biggest, if not the biggest ethnic group in the world to be divided by borders'
sources.source: Kremlin, address on Crimea, English transcript, 18 March 2014

sources.claim: Russia's foreign ministry argues that Estonia's language rules and non-citizen status shut many Russian speakers out of political life, and that Estonia should end both
sources.source: Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, reports on the human rights situation in certain countries (Estonia chapter) and statements on compatriots in the Baltic states

sources.claim: Russia calls the protection of Russian speakers abroad a duty
sources.source: Foreign Policy Concept of the Russian Federation, 31 March 2023 (protection of compatriots abroad)

sources.claim: Roughly 60,000 people in Estonia hold no citizenship
sources.source: Estonian Ministry of the Interior / Police and Border Guard Board, 2024

sources.claim: Estonia says Soviet rule from 1940 to 1991 pushed the Estonian language aside, and its language laws protect it
sources.source: Estonian Ministry of Education and Research, Estonian Language Development Plan; Kasekamp (2010)

sources.claim: Since 2016, children born in Estonia to stateless parents who have lived there legally for at least five years receive citizenship
sources.source: Estonian Citizenship Act amendment, in force 1 January 2016

sources.claim: In August 2022 Estonia moved a Soviet tank monument from near Narva to a museum
sources.source: Estonian Government, 16 August 2022; Estonian War Museum, Viimsi

sources.claim: Schools began moving to Estonian-only teaching from 2024, to finish by 2030
sources.source: Riigikogu, education law amendments, December 2022

sources.claim: In March 2025 Estonia's parliament voted to bar Russian citizens from voting in local elections (the ban applies from later elections)
sources.source: Riigikogu, constitutional amendment adopted 26 March 2025

sources.claim: On 23 May 2024 Russian border guards removed about two dozen of Estonia's buoys on the river
sources.source: Estonian Police and Border Guard Board, 23 May 2024 (24 of about 50)

sources.claim: Russia disputed where the buoys had been placed; Estonia protested
sources.source: Reuters and ERR News, May 2024

sources.claim: The Baltic states disconnected from Russia's grid and joined Europe's on 8-9 February 2025
sources.source: ENTSO-E and Elering, February 2025

sources.claim: Britain leads a NATO battlegroup at Tapa, about 125 km west of Narva
sources.source: NATO Enhanced Forward Presence factsheet; UK Ministry of Defence

sources.claim: Estonia spends more than 3 percent of GDP on defence
sources.source: NATO, Defence Expenditure of NATO Countries, June 2024 estimate (3.43%)

sources.claim: Estonia plans about 600 bunkers under the Baltic Defence Line announced in January 2024
sources.source: Estonian Ministry of Defence, January 2024

sources.claim: Estonia placed dragon's teeth anti-tank blocks near the Narva crossing
sources.source: ERR News, 2024

sources.claim: A 2016 RAND wargame found Russian forces could reach the outskirts of Tallinn and Riga in 36 to 60 hours
sources.source: RAND, Shlapak and Johnson, 'Reinforcing Deterrence on NATO's Eastern Flank', 2016

sources.claim: Many analysts say NATO watches Narva closely and expect the river border to draw closer watching under grey-zone pressure
sources.source: RAND (Shlapak and Johnson, 2016); International Centre for Defence and Security (Tallinn), analyses of Ida-Viru and the Narva border, 2022-2024

sources.claim: Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa operate as road border crossings on the line in use
sources.source: Estonian Police and Border Guard Board, border crossing points, 2024

sources.claim: Finnair paused Tartu flights from 29 April to 31 May 2024 over GPS interference; Estonia blamed Russia
sources.source: Finnair statement, April 2024; Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, May 2024

sources.claim: Transnistria has its own army and currency, hosts Russian troops and is recognised by no UN member
sources.source: OSCE Mission to Moldova; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Transnistria'
